title: A woman gulped ice-cold drinks and ended up with torn arteries
summary: A woman's heart issues seemed to be tied to her rapid gulping of ice-cold drinks.
body: The patient: A 46-year-old woman in California The symptoms: After an uneventful 10-hour work shift, the woman was walking to her car and drinking an ice-cold beverage when a sudden, burning pain struck the middle of her chest. The pain spread to both of her forearms and lasted about 20 minutes. About 10 minutes after this pain began, she started sweating and felt nauseated and lightheaded, as though she might pass out. What happened next: The pain continued as the woman began driving home, so she changed course and instead drove to the nearest emergency department. An electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity, showed subtle abnormalities. A blood test for troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, was normal. However, a second troponin test taken before she left the hospital came back elevated after she had been discharged. Doctors called her about the new results and advised her to drive to the nearest emergency department. title: Scientists put 78,000 letters of human DNA into a mouse — and unraveled how a rare disease worked
summary: By inserting human genes into lab mice, scientists were able to study the underlying mechanics of a disease that's been notoriously difficult to research.
body: Scientists have unraveled the workings of a rare disease by putting a large chunk of human DNA into a lab mouse. The incurable disorder, called X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), mostly affects men of Filipino descent and leads to early death. The new mouse studies revealed previously unknown aspects of the disease's biology that could point to new avenues for treatment. The condition has long been thought of as a disease of neurons, as it triggers neuron death in a part of the brain that's key to controlling movement. But the new findings highlight an unsung role of neurons' support cells, called glial cells. "This had never been described in this disease before," study co-author Shane Liddelow , an associate professor in the Institute for Translational Neuroscience at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, said of the new findings. "It really sort of upended this idea of the disease" as primarily affecting neurons. The two studies, published Thursday (Nov. 19) in the journal Cell, not only shed new light on this rare disease but also showcase a powerful technique for mimicking human conditions in laboratory animals.
